newsitem.title: DUBAI: Arms deal with Qatar seen as coup for Britain.
newsitem.headline: Arms deal with Qatar seen as coup for Britain.

text.p: Britain's $825 million arms deal with Qatar will help it recover lost ground in the Gulf, where leading Western weapons makers are in fierce competition to sell their latest high-tech weaponry to oil-rich customers.
Western diplomats and industry sources described the package as a coup for Britain which has watched the United States and France grab big slices of the lucrative Gulf Arab market.
"This is a good deal for the British. It will help them get back into their traditional pond," said a Western diplomat who closely monitors regional arms sales.
"Especially when you consider that the Americans have gained a big edge after the Gulf War and France's marketing drive and business strategy," he added.
"This is certainly a very good thing for the British," said an American industry source.

Britain and Qatar signed the deal in Doha on Sunday. It involves GKN Piranha armoured personnel carriers, Vosper Thornycroft patrol boats, British Aerospace Hawk training aircraft, and Starburst missiles by Short Missile Systems, a joint venture between Short Brothers and France's Thomson-CSF.
British Defence Secretary Michael Portillo, who signed the package, a month earlier held talks in Qatar and offered the oil and gas-rich state a comprehensive security plan.
Diplomats said the offer was part of a British bid to find a fresh foothold in Gulf Arab states from where it ended 150 years of military protection in 1971.

The United States, France and Britain all have defence pacts with Qatar, whose natural gas reserves -- the world's third largest -- make it one of the most strategic sources of clean energy in the next century.
Gulf Arab security concerns following Iraq's lightning 1990 invasion of Kuwait have turned the region into a high-profit arms bazaar, the industry sources and diplomats say.
The United States, France and Britain are all trying to capitalise on the new security awareness, sending officials to the region and displaying their weaponry at arms shows.
But the diplomats and industry executives say American and French arms makers have gained an edge over the British, once sole protectors of militarily vulnerable Gulf Arab states.
The United States' leading role in ousting Iraqi forces from Kuwait in 1991 has given it an advantage, the sources said.
And France has embarked on an aggressive lobbying campaign filled with protection promises and good bargains that has paid off, the sources added.

Britain earlier this year was squeezed out of a major deal in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) -- now an American and French competition for up to 80 aircraft worth $6 billion -- which could be the last of its size this century.
The UAE, a key buyer in the international arms market, has been haggling with Britain for years over a defence treaty which could help British business in the Gulf Arab state.
British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said earlier this month the two countries were close to agreeing on the pact.
The UAE has defence pacts with the United States and France. It has placed more than $4.3 billion in defence-related orders with the two countries in the past three years.

Britain's deal with Qatar this week could help it regain momentum in the region. It is also competing with American and French arms manufacturers to sell 50 main battle tanks to Qatar's 8,000-man army.
"It will help them get a foothold and reassert their commercial ties to the area," added another Western diplomat.
